rows.passage: In a short fictional scene, a narrator promises to reveal a hidden portrait under a stated condition. A visitor brings a silver token and a folded note, then asks to see the portrait. The scene gives no information about any other visitors. To judge whether the promise applies, use exactly the narrator’s condition rather than assuming that bringing more objects always makes a request more likely to succeed. The narrator says, “I will reveal it if you bring the token, provided you also bring a note.” Apply the promise to this visitor.
rows.segment_text: Apply the promise to this visitor.

rows.passage: A display contains clippings headed Harbor News and Lantern Daily. Students are counting publications rather than individual clippings. A caption explains the relationship between the two headings, which cannot be inferred from their different typefaces alone. Lantern Daily was a separate publication founded alongside Harbor News.
rows.segment_text: Lantern Daily was a separate publication founded alongside Harbor News.

rows.passage: A design class uses two translucent sheets to transfer a pattern. One sheet carries a grid, and the other carries a curved outline. The sheets are named Lake and Hill; these labels do not describe the pattern itself. A student places one sheet above the other and traces the visible marks onto the upper sheet. The direction of copying matters because the exercise records which original design receives the added marks. Lake carries the grid and lies beneath Hill, which carries the outline. Describe the marks copied onto Hill.
rows.segment_text: and the other carries a curved outline.

rows.passage: Call the vertical distance between a floating block’s lower edge and the water surface its immersed depth. A diagram shows the same block floating in two containers, with a ruler beside each container. The containers have different shapes, and their water surfaces appear at different heights on the page. Compare the block’s immersed depth using its lower edge and the local surface in each diagram, rather than comparing the absolute positions of the ruler marks on the page.

A club records the number of puzzles completed by two groups. The smaller group has four members and averages six puzzles per member. The larger group has eight members and averages three puzzles per member. Every member’s completed puzzles count once, and the groups have no members in common. A student proposes averaging the two reported averages without considering how many people belong to each group. Compare the two groups’ reported average numbers of puzzles per member.
